assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the core of modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. Calvo's staggered pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's integrated framework for interest-rate policy are foundational and have changed both research and practice.
assessment.attribution: The field is crowded: Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets all made major contributions, but a cap of three is needed. Calvo (price-setting), Taylor (contracts and rule) and Woodford (synthesis and normative theory) are the most distinct conceptual contributions. Excluding Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
assessment.maturity: Decades of confirmation across academia and central banks, including through the 2008 crisis and the post-2020 inflation. The work is fully mature.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a different trio, such as one including Galí or Christiano and Eichenbaum.
Post-2008 and post-2021 debates may temper views of how well the framework performed.
The risk that many strong contributors cannot all be credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Systematic formal and empirical analysis of how constitutions, electoral rules and political institutions shape fiscal policy, state capacity and economic outcomes. It created a mainstream subfield, political economics, and links closely to growth and development.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini (Political Economics, joint papers on electoral rules and constitutions) are the core. Besley is distinct for the state-capacity and accountability work and is also strongly tied to the field.
assessment.maturity: Work from the 1990s and 2000s with a large literature and well-established empirical follow-up. Timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Acemoglu, Robinson and Johnson won in 2024 for related institutions work, so the Committee may see overlap or a nearby recent prize.
Whether Besley or another figure belongs with the Persson-Tabellini pair.
Cross-country empirical identification remains debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycles model shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It is a workhorse for macro-finance and became central to understanding the financial crisis and the design of macroprudential policy.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 paper is the clear conceptual origin. Gertler and Gilchrist developed the financial-accelerator line (with Bernanke, who was already honored in 2022). Gertler's central-bank work is also credited under B014. I limit the proposal to the two originators.
assessment.maturity: Close to three decades of influence, reinforced by the 2008 crisis and a large quantitative literature. Timing is appropriate.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig on banks and financial crises.
Whether Gertler should be included.
The empirical weight of collateral channels relative to other frictions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BLP methodology for demand estimation in differentiated-product markets, together with dynamic industry models, turned industrial organisation into a quantitative empirical discipline. It is the standard tool in merger analysis, antitrust and many other applied fields.
assessment.attribution: The BLP framework (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) is clearly attributable. Pakes also has distinct contributions on dynamic games (Ericson-Pakes) and estimation. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are significant but less tightly tied to a single breakthrough.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use in research and policy. Fully mature.
uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan and others would be preferred for the earlier empirical-IO contributions.
Methodological rather than substantive discoveries may weigh less with some members.
The three-person cap forces exclusion of Bresnahan.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Misallocation across firms as a quantitative explanation for cross-country income gaps. It transformed development accounting and the empirical study of productivity, and links to growth theory and policy on distortions.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the pivotal paper, with a large follow-up literature. Restuccia and Rogerson's related work is also important, and Restuccia is credited here, but the sharpest empirical identification of the idea is Hsieh-Klenow.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen-plus years of influence. The measurement approach is debated, but the literature is firmly established.
uncertainties: Measurement error and mismeasured markups cast doubt on the size of misallocation estimates.
Priority questions between Restuccia-Rogerson and Hsieh-Klenow.
Whether the contribution is enough of a discovery rather than a measurement application.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence on trade-induced labour-market adjustment reshaped understanding of inequality, polarization and policy. This is close to my own field of technology and inequality, and the work has a large policy and scholarly impact.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure, spanning the task approach (with Levy and Murnane) and the China shock. Hanson and Dorn are tied to the trade-shock papers. Acemoglu's related task-based work is outside this entry's credited names.
assessment.maturity: Task-based work dates from the early 2000s and the China-shock work from 2013 onward. Well established, though some of the long-run interpretation is still debated.
uncertainties: Debate on the persistence and magnitude of China-shock effects.
Overlap with the 2024 prize and the Acemoglu task literature, with possible attribution disputes.
Whether to include Dorn or Katz.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reorganised trade theory around firms, with new gains-from-trade channels. Melitz (2003) is among the most cited trade papers, and the framework spawned a vast empirical and quantitative literature.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the originator. Helpman has broad foundational contributions (monopolistic competition and trade, the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple FDI paper). Redding is important but more recent.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation. Mature.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize covers earlier new trade theory, so the Committee may see an overlap.
Whether Bernard-Jensen empirics deserve credit, since they are not in the credited names.
Helpman also appears under B030.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run series on top incomes and wealth created a new empirical foundation for distribution research, with large influence on public debate and tax policy. The data-construction contribution is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are central to the top-incomes series (with Atkinson, now deceased). Zucman is younger and credited mainly for offshore-wealth work. Saez also appears under B034.
assessment.maturity: Top-income work dates from the early 2000s and is widely replicated. Some of the wealth-concentration estimates remain contested.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over the capital-share and wealth-concentration measures.
The prominent policy and political advocacy may affect how the Committee weighs the scientific record.
Atkinson's death limits credit sharing.
